This was the Children, Young People and Education Committee's last formal business before the Senedd. It was mainly about the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on health and social services as they relate to children and young people in Wales. The team was very pleased to welcome Vaughan Gething AM, the Minister for Health and Social Services; Julie Morgan AM, Deputy Minister for Home and Wales; Nicola Edwards, deputy director, childcare, play and early years; Jean White, chief nursing officer; and Tracey Breheny, who is deputy director of mental health, substance misuse and vulnerable groups. There were lots of questions that they would like to cover, and they would go straight into, with questions from Siân Gwenllian. Then they moved on to some questions on access to health services from Dawn Bowden.

According to Vaughan Gething, they still have seven-day-a-week crisis care. They have also been looking at how that's provided on a phone or online basis where possible, because again the same concerns exist about physical contact with people. They know there is still more to go.

According to Vaughan Gething, the mental health recovery plan would be informed by the understanding of what was happening when they got more engagement with families about the level of need, and then how they needed to think about that. It was a key factor for their return to school, but for the life children and young people led outside the school environment, it would be difficult because they were going to phase out of lockdown—it's not going to be a one-hit measure. They were still committed to it, but again the problem was about the pause or the interruption in work to create the in-patient capacity that they had previously committed to. And they would need to carry on testing themselves and seeing what's happening and looking at the evidence and making sure that the plan they already had got that they published for paediatric critical care was still fit for purpose.

Tracey Breheny first answered that there had been some discharges of young people, but they had had the assurance that that was only undertaken where it was clinically safe to do so and where the community support was in place. In terms of CAMHS primary mental health services, the capacity for in-patients had not been reduced since the beginning of the pandemic, and the CAMHS staff were gradually returning to work from self-isolation or whatever, or from different parts of the system.

According to the statistics, there were more than 1,000 reported suicides in Wales during the COVID-19, and more than half of them were among the children aged 13–18. The group believed that the government had done a lot to tackle the problem, and they had commissioned a national advisory group to review the current, unexpected deaths during the start of the pandemic to understand the wider concerns about the potential effects of the restrictions on the mental health and well-being of children and young people, and if that was leading to a spike in suicide or not. Also, they believed that every case that was known was being RAG rated and services were being linked to that.

According to Vaughan Gething, there still had seven-day-a-week crisis care for children and young people who needed them at the moment. They had built up those crisis care services over a period of time, and the last thing they wanted to see was to see them disappear during this period when there were well-understood concerns about emotional and mental health. They were not services to be scaled down.

According to Vaughan Gething, the perinatal mental health service had not been stopped either. They had also been looking at how that was provided on a phone or online basis where possible, because the same concerns existed about physical contact with people. They knew there was still more to go. It was really impressed by the continuing commitment of the staff to deliver this service for women in what was a particularly uncertain time.

According to Julie Morgan, the definition of vulnerable children and young people included those with a social worker and with statements of special educational needs, and the most vulnerable of these should be prioritized. However, as a result of the outbreak of the coronavirus, there were a whole new group of children that were not necessarily known to services but could still be vulnerable. Therefore, they had set out an expanded definition, which included discretion for local authorities to have some flexibility and to be able to offer a place for those who may be on the edge of receiving care and support if they were known to be vulnerable by the school or by family support services.

Julie Morgan mentioned that a red-amber-green rating risk assessment was adopted by all local authorities at the start of the pandemic to ensure that vulnerable children and families received the right way of receiving services and the frequency of contact from the services. This was being dealt with on a case-by-case basis, so every case that was known was being RAG rated and services were being linked to that.

Julie Morgan had worked with the fostering organizations. They had had close communications with them, and they supported AFA Cymru to develop guidance for foster carers, and that guidance had been very strongly welcomed across the sector. They were also working with the third sector. The Fostering Network had extended its helpline hours, and Voices from Care had developed this particular offer of support for care leavers. So, they had had quite a lot of contact with them.

According to Julie Morgan, the government had taken a very strong line at the beginning that they weren't going to introduce easements in requirements to children's social services. From a Welsh context, the standards that were in place did remain, so therefore there wouldn't have been a necessity for them to do a children's rights impact assessment in relation to the primary legislation. However, as a result of the various coronavirus regulations that they had had, no assessments for children's needs had been postponed, cancelled or done very quickly online rather than in person.

According to Julie Morgan, this was an online survey that they hoped would be going out to thousands of children, and they would get their response in terms of what were the important issues that had arisen for them. What they felt about what's happened during this period, and how they had had to cope in not going school and being at home for so long. And so they were trying to get feedback from young people.

They also moved forward on the wage subsidy and a range of other programs to support workers and small businesses. However, the opposition party argued that the government had not done enough in terms of helping small businesses with the Canada emergency business account, which was another reason why the Covid-19 situation delayed their response. The issue of long-term care was brought up after the military report revealed the appalling conditions experienced by seniors in the care homes. The report stated that cockroaches, flies, mosquitoes, expired medications, unsterile devices and violations of basic contagion rules were among the reasons for the deaths of seniors. The opposition party argued that the for-profit model was failing the seniors and putting profits ahead of the well-being of seniors, while the government argued that it was the duty of the federal government to support the provinces and territories to ensure that every elder person in the community could age with dignity and in safety.

Hon. Patty Hajdu introduced that the government was committed to working with the provinces and territories to ensure that every elder person in the community could age with dignity and in safety. However, as a result of the COVID-19 outbreak, more than 1,000 seniors so far have lost their lives in long-term care homes in Ontario alone, over 25 of them in my riding of MississaugaErin Mills. As a result, the government had stood by Ontario and all of the other provinces during the outbreak.

The opposition party argued that during the pandemic, the government had given money to companies that didn't pay a cent in tax because they used tax havens. The Minister of National Revenue argued that the fight against tax evasion was a priority for the government and they would continue to target companies that used tax evasion schemes. However, the opposition party questioned that the priority had been to protect the employees who worked for the Liberals to ensure their re-election, yet the Liberal Party had raised more than $7million since the last election. The minister argued that it was very important to protect people across the country and in every economic sector that was experiencing a significant drop in income.

Hon. Bill Morneau introduced that the government had put emergency wage subsidy in place in response to the crisis during the pandemic. The wage subsidy was a program that was clearly meant to ensure employees were protected and maintain their relationship with their employer. It was also providing the Canada emergency response benefit to other employees, meaning, those who had lost their income because of COVID-19. The government was working with them through their regional development agencies, and encouraged them to approach their local RDAs, which would be able to help them get the money they deserve.

The debate mainly focused on the issue of the economic bilateral relations with the UK. There was a lot of talk about the Brexit and the potential problems that might affect the bilateral relations between the UK and Canada. As a result of the Brexit, the U.K. would begin applying tariffs at the beginning of next year on Canadian exports such as seafood, beef and cars. The Minister of Foreign Affairs and Chrystia Freeland promised that the government was monitoring the situation very carefully to ensure that CETA continued to apply to the trade with the UK. during this period while they went through Brexit.

Hon. Chrystia Freeland (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Intergovernmental Affairs) introduced that Canada had an excellent assurance of its trade with the United States, which was the new NAFTA trade agreement that they had negotiated, thanks to the unprecedented co-operation across this country. It was very important to the Canadian economy and Canadian producers. However, there was concern that China was procuring and hoarding PPE. Hon. Anita Anand (Minister of Public Services and Procurement) explained that the Government of Canada was operating in a highly competitive global environment, and the reality was that we needed to make sure that we had multiple complementary supply chains operating at the same time, which we had been doing in the past weeks and months, to ensure the front-line health care workers had the supplies they needed to keep Canadians safe.

The senior Canadian bureaucrats received credible reports in early January that China was procuring and hoarding PPE. The government was aware of the challenges the health sector would face, and the government immediately began to work with the provinces and territories to understand what the need would be and how they could best prepare. However, in April, the minister stated there were not enough supplies in the national emergency stockpile. Therefore, the government had to scramble to meet the needs of the front-line health care workers.

Mr. Alain Therrien suggested that during the pandemic, the government gave money to companies that did not pay a cent in tax because they used tax havens. The government responded that it was no big deal. However, it was challenged by Mr. Andrew Scheer that these were very simple technical fixes that could be made by this government. The Minister of National Revenue promised that in everything they do, they would target companies and not innocent workers.

The opposition party pointed out that those who were hardest hit in terms of losing their lives and the negative effects of COVID were the seniors who were living in long-term care homes. The Minister of Families, Children, and Social Development explained that the government had started the process some four years ago when it began to make incredible investments in aging at home. Now, the government was working with the provinces and territories to have a longer-term plan so that all seniors could age with dignity and safety.

Not a single province or territory currently met the benchmark of 4.1 hours of hands-on care per day. As a result Canada had the worst record of COVD-19 deaths among 14 comparable countries, with over 80% of Canadian fatalities occurring in these facilities. The government was committed to working with the provinces and territories to ensure that every elder person in the community could age with dignity and in safety. This was the Children, Young People and Education Committee meeting to discuss the allocation of the higher education new academic year allocations. It was mainly about the financial sustainability of the universities in Wales and the impact of the loss of funds were they to leave the European Union. David Blaney and Bethan Owen were the two leading figures in this meeting, and they were both very pleased to welcome the committee members and the team from the Higher Education Funding Council for Wales. The first question from Lynne Neagle AM focused on the financial indicators for the universities here in Wales, and specifically on the deficit and surpluses of the sector in England. Then, the team discussed the financial support for WISERD Education, which was a research collaboration between a number of the Welsh universities specifically looking at educational issues, and provided additional funding to that to add value to the Welsh Government's existing evaluation of the progress of pioneer schools in developing the three-to-15 curriculum in Wales.

The first was the impact of the demographic dip of 18-year-olds, which is deeper and longer in Wales than it is elsewhere in the UK. The second was the increased pension costs and, actually, increased costs generally. The third was the current uncertainty as a result of the Augar review in England, and whether that might play into Wales, and also Brexit. These challenges were not unique to Wales; the majority of the UK universities were actually taking out cost one way or another. Before the Diamond review of fees and funding in Wales, there was a pre-existing funding gap in resource between England and Wales, which even now, that's still the case. The Welsh higher education institutions were approximately £40 million worse off than they would be in the English system. The money's gone into the system but it hadn't gone into universities, and that was the challenge. They were taking out capacity; they were not cutting at fat now, they were cutting out core capacity.

There were differences in the way that universities had secured funding for investing in their estates. For example, Cardiff University have had a bond rather than borrowing, which they drew down as they were spending. In the short term, the reserves of Cardiff would appear as though they had significant cash balances, but all of those were restricted for investment in the estate and, over the next two or three years, would be utilised for that. Dr David Blaney explained that the estates strategies that institutions operated were overseen by either the full governing body or relevant sub-committees in respect of every institution, so there was proper governance oversight. Also, there was staff and student engagement as well in the strategic approach on estates.

According to Dr David Blaney, the government was not in a managed situation, but the challenges were quite acute. At the moment, they were seeing really challenging circumstances for institutions to manage. One of the things they tried to do was to make sure that, insofar as they could see it, the were making sure that the institutions were alert to the challenges they were facing, and were actually engaging those challenges properly, which was seeing that at the moment. It was not a policy position, and it was not always a good short-term response to crisis anyway, but they were keen to see what they could achieve with the sector in addressing these issues of what constitutes constructive challenge.

The government wanted to ensure that each university's estates strategy and its financing was prudent and had appropriate governing-body oversight in place. It was the big thing that drove most of university borrowing, so it was the government's policy to make sure that the machinery was in place to ensure proper governance oversight. Also, if the institutions were wanting to engage in anything other than relatively trivial borrowing, they had to get the consent of the government.

The institutional risk review process was fundamentally designed to make sure that institutions were grappling with their problems before they became a crisis. 70/80 different factors and hundreds of questions were asked twice a year to interrogate the performance of the institutions. The institutions were asked to think again about some of their aspirations.

It was suggested that more people should be involved in risk management, especially in the institutional risk review process, which has 70/80 different factors and hundreds of questions that are asked twice a year to interrogate the performance of the institutions and to make sure that they are seeing them managing the issues that they're facing.

Dr David Blaney thought it was fair to say that they were seeing an increased risk profile in the sector in Wales, and it was about the financial pressures that they had already discussed this morning. That was why the efforts that the Minister had gone to to secure the Diamond settlement, and, indeed, other bits of money now and again, were so important. The institutions had been working very hard to try not to take cost out now that they really didn't have to take out, because they didn't want to reduce capacity, which they would struggle to recover again when the financial position improved. They were seeing deficits, which were managed deficits, where they were spending more than their income in order just to keep the capacity in.

Bethan Owen thought the key bit of that was maintaining the attractiveness of Welsh universities to students, because a large proportion were coming not from just Wales, but from England and internationally. That's a key part. Also, maintaining the research portfolio was invested in, and that brought economic benefits.

Both the Diamond and Reid reviews called for QR funding to be maintained in real terms, but the allocation for 2019-20 was exactly the same as it had been for the past nine years. The reason the sum had not increased was because they had not had enough money to be able to increase it and still meet the obligations they had to other bits of the HE system. However, they would dearly love to increase the amount.

According to Graeme Reid, there was an assessment of the correlation between QR funding and capacity to generate funding from other sources, and there was a very close correlation. It was sometimes more effective to have external experts making these points than us or the sector.

In 2017-18 and 2018-19, they were providing additional funding to WISERD Education, which was a research collaboration between a number of the Welsh universities, specifically looking at educational issues, to add value to the Welsh Government's existing evaluation of the progress of pioneer schools in developing the three-to-15 curriculum in Wales.

The Reid review had made recommendations to mitigate this impact, including the allocation of additional £6.6 million allocated for research which was put out specifically in line with some of the recommendations from Reid. However, that was not sustainable funding, and it was not enough, really, but it was a good and welcome start. In response to that, the Welsh government had recently issued its own vision for research and innovation, which was developed over a number of months, following the Reid report closely, working with stakeholders and including the Welsh Government, in order to try and set a vision for how to respond to the challenges facing research in the future. Since it seemed possible at least, and possibly even likely, that any money retrieved from not having to invest in the EU would sit in London rather than necessarily being devolved to the devolved administrations, the government had committed in principle to deliver Reid.

The meeting was about a revision of the basic predication of the construction formalism. The document contains two parts, a scenario and a discourse segment. The former is a list of various slots from which to draw in order to paint a picture of what event happened. The latter is a construction of the event that takes place before speech time, and is considered a mental space. It is intended to be used as a sort of evaluative tool. The purpose of the document is to help the team decide what percentage of reality is true and what is not.

The group discussed various strategies for dealing with ambiguity in the semantics of constructions, including focusing on the locus of the goal, meaning bindings, and bindings to ontology items. It was concluded that the full range of semantic structures available to constructions can be used in the semantic side of the model, including constraints, source, path, goal, and constraint bindings. A causal structure for composite events will be discussed in the next meeting.

The semantic specification for the utterance 'big red ball' is derived from the syntactic schemas and bindings to ontology items in the scenario. The intent of the phrase is to know whether there is an object or a noun in the larger context. The entity denoted by the word 'ball' is sort of the semantic head in some ways of the interesting larger element. The semantic value is filled in by sim simulation, but it is still required by simulation time.

The constructions that are in the sentence are supposed to give a cue as to which one of the mental spaces is going to be added. The construction that you actually get is just going to give you a cue of which one you 've already got going , um , you 're supposed to add structure to. This is similar to other kinds of mental space phenomena that can be pulled out of discourse context.

The domain of discourse includes all the interactions that the speaker is supposed to have with other people in the world. In addition, there are many other domains that are not covered in this discussion. These include irony, mockery, etc.
